Part V: Stochastic Methods for Macroeconomic Modeling

kapitaali.com
April 14, 2026

Connects to: Principles Ch. 6, Ch. 15–16, Ch. 20, Appendix B

The models of Parts III and IV are deterministic or, in the case of the RBC model, stochastic in a fully numerical sense — we solved the Bellman equation on a grid without exploiting any linear structure. This part develops the analytical and statistical machinery for handling stochastic models algebraically: rational expectations solution methods, time-series econometrics, the Kalman filter, and structural estimation. These are the tools that connect the theoretical models of Parts III–IV to the data and to the estimation exercises of Part VII.

Chapter 18 solves linear models with forward-looking expectations — the defining feature of New Keynesian macroeconomics. The method of undetermined coefficients (UMC) and McCallum’s minimum-state-variable (MSV) procedure reduce infinite-horizon expectational difference equations to finite-dimensional algebraic problems. Chapter 19 develops the time-series toolkit: unit roots, cointegration, VARs, structural identification, impulse responses, and forecast-error variance decompositions. Chapter 20 derives the Kalman filter from scratch as the MMSE estimator for state-space models, applies it to the output gap and natural rate, and shows how it generates the likelihood function for DSGE estimation. Chapter 21 completes the estimation toolkit with GMM and maximum likelihood, including full asymptotic theory, the delta method, and the application to the consumption Euler equation.

By the end of this part, the reader can take a log-linearized DSGE model (from Part VII), evaluate its likelihood using the Kalman filter, and estimate its parameters via GMM or MLE — the complete estimation pipeline used by every modern central bank model.

Chapter 18: Rational Expectations¶

Solving Linear Expectational Difference Equations

“The assumption of rational expectations is not that agents are geniuses. It is that they are not systematically fooled by the same mistake, period after period.” — Robert Lucas

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 15 (rational expectations definition and the Lucas critique); Ch. 16 (policy ineffectiveness, Barro–Gordon); Ch. 10 (NKPC forward solution as present-value formula) [P:Ch.15, P:Ch.16, P:Ch.10]

18.1 The Rational Expectations Problem¶

Chapter 4 introduced the issue of forward-looking difference equations — equations in which Et[xt+1]\mathbb{E}_t[x_{t+1}]Et​[xt+1​] appears as an argument. Chapter 4’s treatment was informal: we conjectured the MSV solution form and solved for coefficients by matching. This chapter develops the full formal theory.

A rational expectations equilibrium is a stochastic process {xt}\{x_t\}{xt​} such that: (i) households and firms form expectations Et[xt+1]\mathbb{E}_t[x_{t+1}]Et​[xt+1​] as the mathematical conditional expectation given their information set; and (ii) the equilibrium conditions of the model are satisfied. The challenge is that Et[xt+1]\mathbb{E}_t[x_{t+1}]Et​[xt+1​] depends on the equilibrium process for {xt}\{x_t\}{xt​}, which in turn depends on expectations — a circular structure that requires a fixed-point argument to solve.

For linear models, this circular structure can be broken algebraically, yielding closed-form solutions. The tools developed here — undetermined coefficients, the MSV criterion, Blanchard–Kahn counting — are the foundation for Part VII’s DSGE solution algorithms.

18.2 The Scalar Expectational Difference Equation¶

The simplest expectational difference equation:

xt=aEt[xt+1]+bzt,zt=ρzt−1+εt,εt∼WN(0,σ2).x_t = a\mathbb{E}_t[x_{t+1}] + bz_t, \quad z_t = \rho z_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{WN}(0,\sigma^2).xt​=aEt​[xt+1​]+bzt​,zt​=ρzt−1​+εt​,εt​∼WN(0,σ2).
(1)

Here a,ba, ba,b are parameters, ztz_tzt​ is an exogenous AR(1) forcing variable, and xtx_txt​ is the endogenous variable. We seek a solution {xt}\{x_t\}{xt​} consistent with rational expectations.

18.2.1 The Forward Solution¶

Case 1: ∣a∣<1|a| < 1∣a∣<1 (saddle-path stable). Iterate the equation forward:

xt=b∑j=0∞ajEt[zt+j]=b∑j=0∞ajρjzt=b1−aρzt,x_t = b\sum_{j=0}^\infty a^j\mathbb{E}_t[z_{t+j}] = b\sum_{j=0}^\infty a^j\rho^j z_t = \frac{b}{1-a\rho}z_t,xt​=bj=0∑∞​ajEt​[zt+j​]=bj=0∑∞​ajρjzt​=1−aρb​zt​,
(2)

using Et[zt+j]=ρjzt\mathbb{E}_t[z_{t+j}] = \rho^j z_tEt​[zt+j​]=ρjzt​ (the AR(1) forecast). This is the unique bounded solution when ∣a∣<1|a| < 1∣a∣<1 and ∣aρ∣<1|a\rho| < 1∣aρ∣<1.

Case 2: ∣a∣>1|a| > 1∣a∣>1 (indeterminate / forward-explosive). With ∣a∣>1|a| > 1∣a∣>1, the forward iteration diverges unless xtx_txt​ jumps to eliminate the explosive component. Rearrange as Et[xt+1]=xt/a−bzt/a\mathbb{E}_t[x_{t+1}] = x_t/a - bz_t/aEt​[xt+1​]=xt​/a−bzt​/a and substitute the MSV guess xt=ωztx_t = \omega z_txt​=ωzt​:

ωρzt=ωzt/a−bzt/a  ⟹  ω(1/a−ρ)=b/a  ⟹  ω=b1−aρ.\omega\rho z_t = \omega z_t/a - bz_t/a \implies \omega(1/a - \rho) = b/a \implies \omega = \frac{b}{1-a\rho}.ωρzt​=ωzt​/a−bzt​/a⟹ω(1/a−ρ)=b/a⟹ω=1−aρb​.
(3)

Remarkably, the same formula ω=b/(1−aρ)\omega = b/(1-a\rho)ω=b/(1−aρ) applies regardless of whether ∣a∣<1|a| < 1∣a∣<1 or ∣a∣>1|a| > 1∣a∣>1! The distinction is in uniqueness: when ∣a∣<1|a| < 1∣a∣<1 the solution is the unique bounded one; when ∣a∣>1|a| > 1∣a∣>1 there are additional “sunspot” solutions.

18.2.2 Sunspot Solutions and Multiplicity¶

When ∣a∣>1|a| > 1∣a∣>1, the general solution is:

xt=b1−aρzt+ξt,x_t = \frac{b}{1-a\rho}z_t + \xi_t,xt​=1−aρb​zt​+ξt​,
(4)

where ξt\xi_tξt​ is any process satisfying Et[ξt+1]=ξt/a\mathbb{E}_t[\xi_{t+1}] = \xi_t/aEt​[ξt+1​]=ξt​/a. For example, ξt=C⋅a−t\xi_t = C\cdot a^{-t}ξt​=C⋅a−t for any constant CCC is a solution (it dies out monotonically). But also any process with Et[ξt+1]=ξt/a\mathbb{E}_t[\xi_{t+1}] = \xi_t/aEt​[ξt+1​]=ξt​/a works — including sunspot processes driven by extraneous randomness.

Definition 18.1 (Sunspot Equilibrium). A sunspot equilibrium is a rational expectations equilibrium in which the endogenous variable responds to extraneous “sunspot” variables ξt\xi_tξt​ that have no fundamental economic content (they do not affect preferences, technology, or endowments). The sunspot variable satisfies ξt=a−1ξt−1+ηt\xi_t = a^{-1}\xi_{t-1} + \eta_tξt​=a−1ξt−1​+ηt​ where ηt\eta_tηt​ is an arbitrary martingale difference sequence.

When ∣a∣>1|a| > 1∣a∣>1: multiple equilibria (MSV plus any sunspot). When ∣a∣<1|a| < 1∣a∣<1: unique bounded equilibrium (MSV only). This is the scalar analogue of the Blanchard–Kahn counting rule.

18.3 The Method of Undetermined Coefficients (UMC)¶

The UMC provides a systematic procedure for finding the MSV solution of any linear rational expectations model.

Algorithm 18.1 (Method of Undetermined Coefficients).

  1. Identify the state variables — the minimal set st\mathbf{s}_tst​ such that the solution can be written xt=Ωst\mathbf{x}_t = \Omega\mathbf{s}_txt​=Ωst​.

  2. Conjecture the MSV form — xt=Ωst\mathbf{x}_t = \Omega\mathbf{s}_txt​=Ωst​ where Ω\OmegaΩ is an unknown matrix.

  3. Compute Et[xt+1]\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{x}_{t+1}]Et​[xt+1​] — using the law of motion of st\mathbf{s}_tst​: Et[xt+1]=ΩEt[st+1]=ΩΦst\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{x}_{t+1}] = \Omega\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{s}_{t+1}] = \Omega\Phi\mathbf{s}_tEt​[xt+1​]=ΩEt​[st+1​]=ΩΦst​.

  4. Substitute into the model equations.

  5. Match coefficients — equate coefficients of st\mathbf{s}_tst​ on both sides to get a matrix equation for Ω\OmegaΩ.

  6. Solve for Ω\OmegaΩ. Uniqueness of Ω\OmegaΩ is the MSV uniqueness condition.

The matrix equation obtained in step 5 is a Sylvester equation of the form:

Ω=AΩΦ+C,\Omega = A\Omega\Phi + C,Ω=AΩΦ+C,
(5)

where AAA, Φ\PhiΦ, and CCC are known matrices from the model. Vectorizing: vec(Ω)=(I+Φ′⊗A)−1vec(C)\text{vec}(\Omega) = (I + \Phi'\otimes A)^{-1}\text{vec}(C)vec(Ω)=(I+Φ′⊗A)−1vec(C). A unique solution Ω\OmegaΩ exists iff (I+Φ′⊗A)(I + \Phi'\otimes A)(I+Φ′⊗A) is invertible — iff no eigenvalue of Φ\PhiΦ equals the negative of any eigenvalue of AAA, which is generically satisfied.

18.4 The New Keynesian Model: Forward Solutions¶

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 10 (NKPC), Ch. 23 (NK policy) [P:Ch.10, P:Ch.23]

18.4.1 The NKPC as a Forward Equation¶

The New Keynesian Phillips Curve:

π^t=βEt[π^t+1]+κx^t+ut,\hat{\pi}_t = \beta\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] + \kappa\hat{x}_t + u_t,π^t​=βEt​[π^t+1​]+κx^t​+ut​,
(6)

where utu_tut​ is a cost-push shock. This is an expectational difference equation with a=βa = \betaa=β, which satisfies ∣a∣=β<1|a| = \beta < 1∣a∣=β<1. Iterating forward:

π^t=κ∑j=0∞βjEt[x^t+j]+∑j=0∞βjEt[ut+j].\hat{\pi}_t = \kappa\sum_{j=0}^\infty\beta^j\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+j}] + \sum_{j=0}^\infty\beta^j\mathbb{E}_t[u_{t+j}].π^t​=κj=0∑∞​βjEt​[x^t+j​]+j=0∑∞​βjEt​[ut+j​].
(7)

Definition 18.2 (Present-Value Inflation Formula). The NKPC forward solution expresses current inflation as the present discounted value of all future expected output gaps and cost-push shocks:

π^t=κ∑j=0∞βjEt[x^t+j]+∑j=0∞βjEt[ut+j].\hat{\pi}_t = \kappa\sum_{j=0}^\infty\beta^j\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+j}] + \sum_{j=0}^\infty\beta^j\mathbb{E}_t[u_{t+j}].π^t​=κj=0∑∞​βjEt​[x^t+j​]+j=0∑∞​βjEt​[ut+j​].
(8)

This is exactly the formula in Principles Ch. 10.4 [P:Ch.10.4], now derived rigorously. Inflation today depends on the entire expected future path of the output gap — a forward-looking property that makes disinflation potentially costless if it is credible (agents immediately revise down all future inflation expectations).

18.4.2 The NK Three-Equation System Under a Taylor Rule¶

Combine the DIS, NKPC, and Taylor rule from Principles Ch. 23 [P:Ch.23]:

x^t=Et[x^t+1]−σ(i^t−Et[π^t+1]−rtn)(DIS)\hat{x}_t = \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+1}] - \sigma(\hat{i}_t - \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] - r^n_t) \quad \text{(DIS)}x^t​=Et​[x^t+1​]−σ(i^t​−Et​[π^t+1​]−rtn​)(DIS)
(9)
π^t=βEt[π^t+1]+κx^t(NKPC)\hat{\pi}_t = \beta\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] + \kappa\hat{x}_t \quad \text{(NKPC)}π^t​=βEt​[π^t+1​]+κx^t​(NKPC)
(10)
i^t=ϕππ^t+ϕyx^t(Taylor rule)\hat{i}_t = \phi_\pi\hat{\pi}_t + \phi_y\hat{x}_t \quad \text{(Taylor rule)}i^t​=ϕπ​π^t​+ϕy​x^t​(Taylor rule)
(11)

with exogenous shocks: rtn=ρrrt−1n+εtrr^n_t = \rho_r r^n_{t-1} + \varepsilon^r_trtn​=ρr​rt−1n​+εtr​ (demand shock).

Step 1: Substitute the Taylor rule into the DIS:

x^t=Et[x^t+1]−σϕππ^t−σϕyx^t+σEt[π^t+1]+σrtn.\hat{x}_t = \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+1}] - \sigma\phi_\pi\hat{\pi}_t - \sigma\phi_y\hat{x}_t + \sigma\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] + \sigma r^n_t.x^t​=Et​[x^t+1​]−σϕπ​π^t​−σϕy​x^t​+σEt​[π^t+1​]+σrtn​.
(12)

Collecting x^t\hat{x}_tx^t​:

(1+σϕy)x^t=Et[x^t+1]+σEt[π^t+1]−σϕππ^t+σrtn.(1+\sigma\phi_y)\hat{x}_t = \mathbb{E}_t[\hat{x}_{t+1}] + \sigma\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] - \sigma\phi_\pi\hat{\pi}_t + \sigma r^n_t.(1+σϕy​)x^t​=Et​[x^t+1​]+σEt​[π^t+1​]−σϕπ​π^t​+σrtn​.
(13)

Step 2: Stack the system. Let yt=(π^t,x^t)′\mathbf{y}_t = (\hat{\pi}_t, \hat{x}_t)'yt​=(π^t​,x^t​)′ and zt=rtnz_t = r^n_tzt​=rtn​. Write in the canonical form:

(1−κσϕπ1+σϕy)⏟≡Γ0yt=(β0−σ1)⏟≡Γ1Et[yt+1]+(0σ)⏟≡Ψzt.\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}1 & -\kappa \\ \sigma\phi_\pi & 1+\sigma\phi_y\end{pmatrix}}_{\equiv\Gamma_0}\mathbf{y}_t = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\beta & 0 \\ -\sigma & 1\end{pmatrix}}_{\equiv\Gamma_1}\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] + \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ \sigma\end{pmatrix}}_{\equiv\Psi}z_t.≡Γ0​(1σϕπ​​−κ1+σϕy​​)​​yt​=≡Γ1​(β−σ​01​)​​Et​[yt+1​]+≡Ψ(0σ​)​​zt​.
(14)

Step 3: Reduce to standard form. Pre-multiply by Γ0−1\Gamma_0^{-1}Γ0−1​:

yt=Γ0−1Γ1⏟≡AEt[yt+1]+Γ0−1Ψ⏟≡Czt.\mathbf{y}_t = \underbrace{\Gamma_0^{-1}\Gamma_1}_{\equiv A}\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] + \underbrace{\Gamma_0^{-1}\Psi}_{\equiv C}z_t.yt​=≡AΓ0−1​Γ1​​​Et​[yt+1​]+≡CΓ0−1​Ψ​​zt​.
(15)

Step 4: Apply UMC. Guess yt=Ωzt\mathbf{y}_t = \Omega z_tyt​=Ωzt​. Then Et[yt+1]=Ωρrzt\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] = \Omega\rho_r z_tEt​[yt+1​]=Ωρr​zt​. Substituting:

Ωzt=AΩρrzt+Czt  ⟹  Ω=AΩρr+C.\Omega z_t = A\Omega\rho_r z_t + Cz_t \implies \Omega = A\Omega\rho_r + C.Ωzt​=AΩρr​zt​+Czt​⟹Ω=AΩρr​+C.
(16)

This is the Sylvester equation for a 2×12\times12×1 matrix Ω\OmegaΩ (since ztz_tzt​ is scalar):

Ω(I−Aρr)=C  ⟹  Ω=C(I−Aρr)−1.\Omega(I - A\rho_r) = C \implies \Omega = C(I - A\rho_r)^{-1}.Ω(I−Aρr​)=C⟹Ω=C(I−Aρr​)−1.
(17)

This requires (I−Aρr)(I - A\rho_r)(I−Aρr​) to be invertible — satisfied generically.

Step 5: Verify determinacy. The solution Ω\OmegaΩ is the unique MSV solution iff the NK system has a unique bounded equilibrium. For a system with two free (forward-looking) variables (π^t,x^t)(\hat\pi_t, \hat{x}_t)(π^t​,x^t​), the Blanchard–Kahn condition requires two eigenvalues of A=Γ0−1Γ1A = \Gamma_0^{-1}\Gamma_1A=Γ0−1​Γ1​ outside the unit circle.

Theorem 18.1 (Taylor Principle and Determinacy). In the NK three-equation model, the Blanchard–Kahn condition is satisfied — the equilibrium is unique — if and only if:

ϕπ+1−βκϕy>1.\phi_\pi + \frac{1-\beta}{\kappa}\phi_y > 1.ϕπ​+κ1−β​ϕy​>1.
(18)

For ϕy=0\phi_y = 0ϕy​=0: the condition reduces to ϕπ>1\phi_\pi > 1ϕπ​>1, the Taylor principle: the central bank must raise the nominal rate by more than one-for-one with inflation.

Proof sketch. The determinant and trace of A=Γ0−1Γ1A = \Gamma_0^{-1}\Gamma_1A=Γ0−1​Γ1​ can be computed explicitly. The eigenvalue analysis shows that both eigenvalues of AAA have modulus greater than 1 iff the stated condition holds. See Chapter 28 for the full proof using the QZ decomposition. □\square□

18.5 Sunspots and Indeterminacy in the NK Model¶

When ϕπ<1\phi_\pi < 1ϕπ​<1 (Taylor principle violated), the NK model has indeterminate equilibria: the MSV solution is one equilibrium, but there are infinitely many others driven by sunspot shocks. The general solution is:

π^t=ωπzt+ξt,x^t=ωxzt+φξt,\hat{\pi}_t = \omega_\pi z_t + \xi_t, \quad \hat{x}_t = \omega_x z_t + \varphi\xi_t,π^t​=ωπ​zt​+ξt​,x^t​=ωx​zt​+φξt​,
(19)

where ξt\xi_tξt​ is an arbitrary sunspot process satisfying Et[ξt+1]=ξt/λ+\mathbb{E}_t[\xi_{t+1}] = \xi_t/\lambda_+Et​[ξt+1​]=ξt​/λ+​ (where λ+<1\lambda_+ < 1λ+​<1 is the eigenvalue of AAA inside the unit circle) and φ\varphiφ is a coefficient determined by the eigenvector.

Economic implication: Sunspot equilibria generate volatility unrelated to fundamentals — the economy can fluctuate even when technology, preferences, and government policy are perfectly stable. The Taylor principle (ϕπ>1\phi_\pi > 1ϕπ​>1) rules out sunspots by ensuring both eigenvalues of AAA lie outside the unit circle, leaving the MSV solution as the unique equilibrium [P:Ch.23.1].

18.6 Worked Example: Impulse Response to a Cost-Push Shock¶

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 10.3, Ch. 23.2 [P:Ch.10.3, P:Ch.23.2]

Calibration: β=0.99\beta = 0.99β=0.99, κ=0.15\kappa = 0.15κ=0.15, σ=1\sigma = 1σ=1, ϕπ=1.5\phi_\pi = 1.5ϕπ​=1.5, ϕy=0.5\phi_y = 0.5ϕy​=0.5, ρr=0\rho_r = 0ρr​=0 (i.i.d. shock, so rtn=εtrr^n_t = \varepsilon^r_trtn​=εtr​).

Add a cost-push shock ut=ρuut−1+εtuu_t = \rho_u u_{t-1} + \varepsilon^u_tut​=ρu​ut−1​+εtu​ with ρu=0.5\rho_u = 0.5ρu​=0.5.

State: st=(rtn,ut)′\mathbf{s}_t = (r^n_t, u_t)'st​=(rtn​,ut​)′. Augment the NKPC: π^t=βEt[π^t+1]+κx^t+ut\hat{\pi}_t = \beta\mathbb{E}_t[\hat{\pi}_{t+1}] + \kappa\hat{x}_t + u_tπ^t​=βEt​[π^t+1​]+κx^t​+ut​.

MSV guess: yt=Ωst\mathbf{y}_t = \Omega\mathbf{s}_tyt​=Ωst​ where Ω\OmegaΩ is 2×22\times22×2.

The Sylvester equation Ω=AΩΦ+C\Omega = A\Omega\Phi + CΩ=AΩΦ+C where Φ=diag(ρr,ρu)=diag(0,0.5)\Phi = \text{diag}(\rho_r, \rho_u) = \text{diag}(0, 0.5)Φ=diag(ρr​,ρu​)=diag(0,0.5) and CCC now has a second column for utu_tut​.

Python¶

import numpy as np

beta, kappa, sigma, phi_pi, phi_y = 0.99, 0.15, 1.0, 1.5, 0.5
rho_u, rho_r = 0.5, 0.0

# Structural matrices
G0 = np.array([[1, -kappa], [sigma*phi_pi, 1+sigma*phi_y]])
G1 = np.array([[beta, 0], [-sigma, 1]])
A  = np.linalg.inv(G0) @ G1

# Check Taylor principle
eigs = np.linalg.eigvals(A)
print(f"Eigenvalues of A: {np.abs(eigs)}  (both > 1: {np.all(np.abs(eigs)>1)})")

# Shock loadings (C matrix)
G0_inv = np.linalg.inv(G0)
Psi = np.array([[1, 0], [0, sigma]])  # [u in NKPC, r^n in DIS]
C = G0_inv @ Psi

# State transition matrix
Phi = np.diag([rho_u, rho_r])

# Sylvester equation: Omega = A @ Omega @ Phi + C
# Vectorized: (I - Phi' ⊗ A) vec(Omega) = vec(C)
from numpy import kron
KronPA = np.kron(Phi.T, A)
I4 = np.eye(4)
vec_Omega = np.linalg.solve(I4 - KronPA, C.flatten(order='F'))
Omega = vec_Omega.reshape(2, 2, order='F')
print(f"\nMSV solution matrix Ω:\n{np.round(Omega,3)}")
print(f"Interpretation: π̂_t = {Omega[0,0]:.3f}·u_t + {Omega[0,1]:.3f}·r^n_t")
print(f"                x̂_t = {Omega[1,0]:.3f}·u_t + {Omega[1,1]:.3f}·r^n_t")

# Impulse responses to cost-push shock u (column 0 of Omega × Phi^h × e_u)
H = 20
e_u = np.array([1, 0])  # unit shock to u
irf_pi = np.zeros(H); irf_x = np.zeros(H)
state = e_u.copy()
for h in range(H):
    response = Omega @ state
    irf_pi[h] = response[0]; irf_x[h] = response[1]
    state = Phi @ state

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=(10,4))
ax1.bar(range(H), irf_pi, color='steelblue')
ax1.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.5); ax1.set_title('Inflation IRF (cost-push shock)')
ax1.set_xlabel('Quarters')
ax2.bar(range(H), irf_x, color='tomato')
ax2.axhline(0, color='k', lw=0.5); ax2.set_title('Output gap IRF (cost-push shock)')
ax2.set_xlabel('Quarters')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Julia¶

using LinearAlgebra

beta, kappa, sigma, phi_pi, phi_y = 0.99, 0.15, 1.0, 1.5, 0.5
rho_u, rho_r = 0.5, 0.0

G0 = [1 -kappa; sigma*phi_pi 1+sigma*phi_y]
G1 = [beta 0; -sigma 1]
A  = inv(G0) * G1

eigs = eigvals(A)
println("Eigenvalues of A: $(round.(abs.(eigs),digits=3)) (>1: $(all(abs.(eigs).>1)))")

G0_inv = inv(G0)
Psi = [1 0; 0 sigma]
C = G0_inv * Psi
Phi = diagm([rho_u, rho_r])

# Sylvester: Ω = A*Ω*Φ + C → (I - Φ'⊗A)vec(Ω) = vec(C)
KronPA = kron(Phi', A)
I4 = I(4)
vec_Omega = (I4 - KronPA) \ vec(C)
Omega = reshape(vec_Omega, 2, 2)

println("\nΩ (MSV solution):\n", round.(Omega, digits=3))

# IRF to unit cost-push shock
H = 20
irf = [Omega * (Phi^h * [1.0, 0.0]) for h in 0:H-1]
pi_irf = [r[1] for r in irf]
x_irf  = [r[2] for r in irf]
println("\nInflation IRF (first 5): $(round.(pi_irf[1:5], digits=3))")
println("Output IRF   (first 5): $(round.(x_irf[1:5],  digits=3))")

R¶

beta<-0.99; kappa<-0.15; sigma<-1; phi_pi<-1.5; phi_y<-0.5
rho_u<-0.5; rho_r<-0.0

G0 <- matrix(c(1,sigma*phi_pi,-kappa,1+sigma*phi_y),2,2)
G1 <- matrix(c(beta,-sigma,0,1),2,2)
A  <- solve(G0) %*% G1

eigs <- eigen(A)$values
cat(sprintf("Eigenvalue moduli: %.3f, %.3f  (Taylor principle: %s)\n",
            Mod(eigs[1]), Mod(eigs[2]), all(Mod(eigs)>1)))

Psi <- matrix(c(1,0,0,sigma),2,2)
C   <- solve(G0) %*% Psi
Phi <- diag(c(rho_u, rho_r))

# Sylvester equation (using vec and Kronecker)
KronPA <- kronecker(t(Phi), A)
I4 <- diag(4)
vec_Omega <- solve(I4 - KronPA, as.vector(C))
Omega <- matrix(vec_Omega, 2, 2)
cat("\nΩ (MSV solution):\n"); print(round(Omega,3))

# IRF
H <- 20
state <- c(1, 0)
pi_irf <- x_irf <- numeric(H)
for(h in 1:H) {
  resp <- Omega %*% state; pi_irf[h] <- resp[1]; x_irf[h] <- resp[2]
  state <- Phi %*% state
}
cat("\nInflation IRF (first 5):", round(pi_irf[1:5],3))

18.7 Programming Exercises¶

Exercise 18.1 (APL — Determinacy Region)¶

Compute the determinacy region in (ϕπ,ϕy)(\phi_\pi, \phi_y)(ϕπ​,ϕy​) space for the NK model. For each pair (ϕπ,ϕy)(\phi_\pi, \phi_y)(ϕπ​,ϕy​) on a 20×2020\times2020×20 grid over [0,3]×[0,1.5][0, 3]\times[0, 1.5][0,3]×[0,1.5]: (a) compute A=Γ0−1Γ1A = \Gamma_0^{-1}\Gamma_1A=Γ0−1​Γ1​; (b) compute the eigenvalue moduli; (c) flag as determinate if both moduli exceed 1. Display as an APL Boolean matrix and verify the boundary matches ϕπ+(1−β)ϕy/κ=1\phi_\pi + (1-\beta)\phi_y/\kappa = 1ϕπ​+(1−β)ϕy​/κ=1.

Exercise 18.2 (Python — Forward Guidance)¶

“Forward guidance” is a commitment to keep rates at zero for TTT periods beyond when liftoff would normally occur. In the NK model, this means setting i^t=0\hat{i}_t = 0i^t​=0 for t=0,…,T−1t = 0, \ldots, T-1t=0,…,T−1 and returning to the Taylor rule at t=Tt = Tt=T. (a) Solve the model recursively backward from t=Tt = Tt=T (where the Taylor rule applies) to t=0t = 0t=0 (where the peg applies). (b) Plot the impulse response of inflation and the output gap at t=0t = 0t=0 as a function of TTT for T∈{1,2,4,8}T \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}T∈{1,2,4,8}. (c) Observe the “forward guidance puzzle”: the effect grows exponentially in TTT for standard calibrations.

Exercise 18.3 (Julia — Sunspot Volatility)¶

# Compare fundamental vs. sunspot volatility
beta, kappa, sigma = 0.99, 0.15, 1.0

# Indeterminate calibration: phi_pi = 0.8 (below Taylor principle)
phi_pi_ind = 0.8; phi_y_ind = 0.0
G0_ind = [1 -kappa; sigma*phi_pi_ind 1+sigma*phi_y_ind]
G1_ind = [beta 0; -sigma 1]
A_ind  = inv(G0_ind) * G1_ind
eig_ind = eigvals(A_ind)
println("Indeterminate eigenvalues: $(round.(abs.(eig_ind),digits=3))")
# One eigenvalue inside unit circle → sunspots possible
lam_inside = eig_ind[argmin(abs.(eig_ind))]
println("Inside eigenvalue λ = $(round(lam_inside,digits=3))")
println("Sunspot process: ξ_t = $(round(1/abs(lam_inside),digits=3))·ξ_{t-1} + η_t")

Exercise 18.4 — Hybrid NKPC (⋆\star⋆)¶

The hybrid NKPC (Galí and Gertler, 1999) has both forward- and backward-looking components:

π^t=ωfβEt[π^t+1]+ωbπ^t−1+κx^t,ωf+ωb=1.\hat\pi_t = \omega_f\beta\mathbb{E}_t[\hat\pi_{t+1}] + \omega_b\hat\pi_{t-1} + \kappa\hat{x}_t, \quad \omega_f + \omega_b = 1.π^t​=ωf​βEt​[π^t+1​]+ωb​π^t−1​+κx^t​,ωf​+ωb​=1.
(20)

Now π^t−1\hat\pi_{t-1}π^t−1​ is a predetermined state variable. (a) Write the system in the form yt=AEt[yt+1]+Byt−1+Czt\mathbf{y}_t = A\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] + B\mathbf{y}_{t-1} + C\mathbf{z}_tyt​=AEt​[yt+1​]+Byt−1​+Czt​ with yt=(π^t,x^t)′\mathbf{y}_t = (\hat\pi_t, \hat{x}_t)'yt​=(π^t​,x^t​)′. (b) The system now has one predetermined variable (π^t−1\hat\pi_{t-1}π^t−1​) and two jump variables; the Blanchard–Kahn condition requires exactly one eigenvalue inside the unit circle. (c) Solve using the MSV approach and compare IRFs to the pure NKPC case.

18.8 Chapter Summary¶

Key results:

  • The scalar expectational equation xt=aEt[xt+1]+bztx_t = a\mathbb{E}_t[x_{t+1}] + bz_txt​=aEt​[xt+1​]+bzt​ has MSV solution xt=[b/(1−aρ)]ztx_t = [b/(1-a\rho)]z_txt​=[b/(1−aρ)]zt​, valid whenever ∣aρ∣≠1|a\rho| \neq 1∣aρ∣=1; unique bounded solution iff ∣a∣<1|a| < 1∣a∣<1; multiple solutions (sunspots) iff ∣a∣>1|a| > 1∣a∣>1.

  • The method of undetermined coefficients: conjecture yt=Ωst\mathbf{y}_t = \Omega\mathbf{s}_tyt​=Ωst​, substitute, match coefficients to get the Sylvester equation Ω=AΩΦ+C\Omega = A\Omega\Phi + CΩ=AΩΦ+C, solve via vec(Ω)=(I−Φ′⊗A)−1vec(C)\text{vec}(\Omega) = (I-\Phi'\otimes A)^{-1}\text{vec}(C)vec(Ω)=(I−Φ′⊗A)−1vec(C).

  • The NK model in canonical form yt=AEt[yt+1]+Czt\mathbf{y}_t = A\mathbb{E}_t[\mathbf{y}_{t+1}] + C\mathbf{z}_tyt​=AEt​[yt+1​]+Czt​ is determinate iff both eigenvalues of A=Γ0−1Γ1A = \Gamma_0^{-1}\Gamma_1A=Γ0−1​Γ1​ lie outside the unit circle — the Blanchard–Kahn condition with nf=2n_f = 2nf​=2 free variables.

  • The Taylor principle (ϕπ+(1−β)ϕy/κ>1\phi_\pi + (1-\beta)\phi_y/\kappa > 1ϕπ​+(1−β)ϕy​/κ>1) is necessary and sufficient for determinacy in the NK model.

  • In APL: the Kronecker product is Phi_t kron A via outer product ∘.×; the Sylvester system is solved by vec_C ⌹ I4 - KronPA; IRFs are {Omega +.× Phi⍣⍵ +.× e_shock}¨⍳H.
